extracted.intended_audience: grant reviewers and researchers working on biofilm mechanics, microbiology, and host–pathogen interactions
extracted.subtask_description: A research strategy from an NIH-style grant describing experiments to characterize structural, mechanical, and biological properties of Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm infections and their impact on antibiotic tolerance and neutrophil interactions. Includes in vivo, ex vivo, and in vitro methods, expected outcomes, pitfalls, and animal-use details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex vivo AFM mechanical characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary mechanical characterization of in-vivo wound biofilms will be through ex-vivo measurements using an AFM on biopsies harvested from mouse wound beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place biopsies onto an agar plate submerged in growth broth and keep samples in liquid environment; probe 2D areas from ~100 µm lateral dimensions to much larger; perform all tests as quickly as possible after excision (always <12 hours). Use an Asylum Research MFP-3D SA AFM in liquid.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFM tapping mode for topography and stiffness mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AFM in tapping mode to determine topography and locate biofilm regions and obtain qualitative stiffness map to distinguish biofilm from tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tapping mode provides topographical height map and qualitative stiffness mapping; use this to identify regions for detailed mechanical probing [153-155].

rubrics_metrics.name: AFM Force-Volume mapping and contact-model elasticity estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform Force-Volume mapping by rastering the AFM tip over the 2D sample to obtain force-displacement curves and compute elasticity using appropriate contact models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a cantilever with a round, large silica probe. Typically use Hertz or Sneddon models assuming no adhesion, but alternative models including adhesion are available for biological samples [100,153-156].

rubrics_metrics.name: AFM constant-force mode to obtain relaxation spectrum and viscosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Run AFM in constant force mode while measuring displacement to yield the relaxation time spectrum and estimate viscosity by assuming a Maxwell element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure displacement under constant force to derive relaxation times; interpret viscosity by modeling biofilm as spring+dashpot in series (Maxwell).

rubrics_metrics.name: AFM amplitude & frequency modulation for viscoelastic moduli (G' and G'')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use amplitude and frequency modulation AFM to obtain in situ, high-spatial-resolution measurements of viscoelastic G' and G''. Rastering will provide maps of these moduli comparable to rheometer results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force cantilever to vibrate at controlled frequency and amplitude before contact; relate amplitude and frequency changes caused by biofilm to viscoelastic moduli. This mode runs automatically on the AFM and yields rheometer-like results [153].

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain near in-vivo state during ex vivo testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep excised biofilm samples submerged and tested in liquid to ensure measurements reflect the in-vivo state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submerge samples in growth broth on agar and test within 12 hours of excision to minimize ex vivo artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt in vivo microrheology as complementary technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Where feasible, attempt in vivo microrheology (passive two-particle and active magnetic bead-based) to validate ex vivo AFM measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-particle passive microrheology via cross-correlated thermal motion of colloids and high-speed 3D confocal imaging; if tracer particles incorporate, use magnetic beads and magnetic tweezers (stresses up to ~25 kPa) for active microrheology. Note: in vivo microrheology is challenging and is a secondary/supplemental technique [157-161].

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate non-EPS causes for mechanical/structural changes
rubrics_metrics.description: If measured changes in structure or mechanics do not correlate with EPS or protein content, investigate alternative causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider varying pH, salt concentration, cross-linking by pili/flagella, degradation by host enzymes, or effects from reactive oxygen species from neutrophils [103,162].

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreate salient structural features in vitro to study microenvironments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recreate key structural characteristics (aggregate size, inter-aggregate spacing, matrix heterogeneity) in vitro to measure resulting oxygen gradients, antibiotic resistance, virulence, and quorum sensing in microenvironments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use optical trapping, 3D gels, and µ3D printing to mimic in vivo structures; rationale is to link structure to clinical-relevant outcomes and identify when structure-targeting treatments are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use optical trapping to build controlled 3D biofilm structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use optical trapping to create user-controlled biofilm structures with single-cell resolution and co-patterning of strains to reproduce in vivo-like suspended aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optical trapping allows construction without enclosing bacteria and reproduces sizes comparable to in vivo aggregates; preferable where aggregates are suspended (e.g., wound infections) [9,15,202,203].

rubrics_metrics.name: Use suspended aggregates in agarose/agar gels to mimic diffusive transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Grow suspended bacterial aggregates in soft 3D gels (agarose/agar) to better re-create diffusive transport-dominated wound environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary initial bacterial number density to control inter-aggregate spacing; aggregate size varies with distance to nutrient interface; gels allow higher throughput than optical trapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use µ3D printing to restrict physical/chemical access for signaling vs transport tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use µ3D printed picoliter microenclosures (walls from cross-linked proteins) to encapsulate bacteria and control diffusion, thereby distinguishing transport-mediated from signaling-mediated EPS effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walls provide physical boundaries supporting diffusion depending on matrix composition and crosslinking; useful to isolate transport phenomena from EPS-induced signaling [196,197,210].

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopy and sensor measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use wide-field epifluorescence, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), fiber optic and electrochemical microsensors for measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure antibiotic resistance with live-dead staining; measure quorum sensing and virulence with GFP reporter strains (rsaL and rhl); measure metabolically-active cells via a GFP plasmid expressed only in active cells and use quantitative FISH; measure oxygen and pH with microsensors [12,214-217,212,213].

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify in vitro relevance by comparison to in vivo outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare in vitro results (structure effects on physiology, resistance, virulence) to disease outcomes observed in Specific Aim 1 to confirm in vivo relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design in vitro assays to reproduce structural metrics measured in vivo (Activity 1.1) and validate by outcome comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure antibiotic distributions and endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess antibiotic distribution and bactericidal effect as primary endpoints for antibiotic-tolerance experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fluorescently-tagged drugs and hydrophilic fluorophores to map antibiotic distribution; endpoints are killing of bacteria, or achieving steady-state antibiotic distributions if killing does not occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use core–shell µ3D-printed communities to test EPS-mediated protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Encapsulate EPS non-producers in cores surrounded by shells containing EPS producers or EPS extracts to test whether EPS protects via transport-hindering rather than direct cell contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tune shell thickness, composition, and cross-linking to be permeable to antibiotics but impermeable to high molecular-weight EPS. Optionally eliminate outer shell to simulate producers in bulk solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control experiments and genetic controls for quorum sensing/virulence assays
rubrics_metrics.description: Use GFP reporter strains to measure quorum-sensing-mediated virulence and include mutants incapable of responding to quorum sensing as controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also use strains that constitutively overexpress rhamnolipids/pyocyanin and strains with inducible virulence to probe virulence–structure relationships; expect trade-off between cell density (autoinducer concentration) and low metabolism in large aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model virulence-mediated killing with Hill dose–response and dose-response surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze virulence factor killing using Hill functions and multi-dimensional dose-response surfaces to capture interactions between multiple virulence factors and between mechanics and virulence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat timescale for phagocytic engulfment as one 'concentration' axis when analyzing interactions between mechanics and virulence; expect additive or synergistic interactions, analogous to antibiotic interaction analyses [13,259-264].

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreate gel mechanical properties (G', σY, εY) relevant to biofilms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use agarose and polyacrylamide gels to reproduce ranges of elastic modulus G', yield stress σY, and yield strain εY measured for biofilms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tune agarose via concentration and molecular weight (below 1 kPa to >1 MPa); tune polyacrylamide via acrylamide/bis-acrylamide (0.5–50 kPa). Extend to alginate/other hydrogels if softer materials needed [246-249,265-269].

rubrics_metrics.name: Phagocytosis assays using neutrophils and gel targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Add freshly-isolated human neutrophils to gels (with embedded bacteria) and assess phagocytic susceptibility using high-throughput fluorescence and microscopy-based assays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assay 1: Multi-well plates coated with gel containing fluorescent beads; measure neutrophil fluorescence via plate reader or flow cytometer as proxy for phagocytosis and measure gel volume change. Assay 2: Microscopy at 37°C on gel-coated coverslips to record interactions and use beads/bacteria for traction force microscopy to measure stresses/strains/yielding/engulfment [83,250,251].

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized relationships between mechanics and phagocytosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect susceptibility to phagocytosis to decrease with increasing G' and σY for long incubations, with windows of mechanics where disrupting mechanics could increase susceptibility; expect timescale to complete phagocytosis to increase with εY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracket mechanical 'windows' (G', σY, εY) where interventions are likely effective; if relationships do not fit εY/σY, examine viscous contributions to an 'EnergyY' metric and measure variation in stresses exerted by phagocytes as a function of substrate G'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate in vivo by implanting gel beads with defined phagocytic susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Create bacteria-impregnated gel beads representing extremes of phagocytic susceptibility and timescale, inoculate into mouse wounds, and measure inflammation, wound closure/healing, and bacterial load at defined timepoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both WT and highly virulent strains to probe interplay of mechanics and virulence; measure outcomes at 4 and 7 days post-inoculation to assess impact on disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing potential pitfalls with alternative materials and adhesion testing
rubrics_metrics.description: If gels resist phagocytosis despite provoking immune responses, test whether stiffness or yield stress is too high and extend assays to softer hydrogels; measure adhesive forces between neutrophils and biofilms if mechanics appear non-contributory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alginate and other softer hydrogels if needed; use AFM and shear flow to measure adhesion strength—anticipate stronger adhesion correlating with greater phagocytosis probability [265-269,270].

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded experimental design for bacterial strain identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement blinded studies by coding bacterial strains so that researchers performing experiments/analysis do not know strain identity until completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code strains for collaborators (e.g., Texas Tech researchers) to reduce bias during experiments and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal use compliance and approved protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct all animal experiments in strict accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals under approved IACUC protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocol was approved by Texas Tech University HSC IACUC (Protocol Number: 07044); follow stated procedures for anesthesia, wounding, infection, dressings, fluid replacement, and recovery to create chronic non-lethal wound model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified vertebrate-animal model and surgical protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Use adult female Swiss Webster mice in a non-lethal full-thickness dorsal excisional skin wound model infected with ~10^5 CFU and covered with semipermeable polyurethane dressing to model chronic wounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anesthetize with intraperitoneal pentobarbital, create 1.0 x 1.0 cm wound to panniculus muscle, inoculate bacteria, cover with OPSITE dressing to prevent contractile healing, provide warmed lactated Ringer's and recovery under warming lights; model yields persistent infection recalcitrant to antibiotics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project management and collaboration structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Define roles and oversight for PI and collaborators, meeting cadence, and reporting expectations to ensure coordinated execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PI (V. Gordon) leads collaboration, supervises specified activities; named collaborators supervise animal work, ex vivo measurements, µ3D-printing. Students/senior personnel meet yearly in person, Skype monthly, and students prepare written bimonthly reports; joint manuscript preparation noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of outcome to guide later aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the comprehensive mechanical and structural knowledge outcomes from Aim 1 and Aim 2 to guide interventions in later aims and the overall project direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected outcomes include identification of mechanical and structural windows that influence antibiotic tolerance, virulence, and immune evasion, enabling design of mechanics- or structure-targeting strategies to improve clearance.
